categoryCoverage.note: No owner/admin role or privileged function exists in this contract; liquidate() is intentionally permissionless.

This contract implements no flash-loan API itself; the flash-loan-facilitated exploitation route against the external AMM pair is analyzed under the SC03 spot-price-oracle-manipulation finding rather than as a separate finding.
The sole external call (getReserves) is read-only, forwards no value, and its return values are consumed rather than silently discarded; its risk as an untrusted data source is captured under SC03.
Every division is preceded by its multiplication, and the liquidation comparison cross-multiplies instead of dividing, avoiding precision loss.
liquidate() zeroes state before the ETH transfer (correct checks-effects-interactions) and uses transfer(), which forwards a fixed 2300 gas stipend; no reentrancy path is present.

Solidity 0.8.20's built-in overflow checks are active and no unchecked blocks are used; the arithmetic-revert-driven denial of service this enables (via the uncapped borrow amount) is reported under SC02 instead.

findings.description: The collateral price used for liquidation decisions is computed directly from the instantaneous reserves of a single AMM pair (getReserves), as reserve1/reserve0, with no time-weighting, no staleness check against the returned blockTimestampLast (which is read and immediately discarded), and no deviation/sanity bound. This spot price feeds straight into isLiquidatable(), which gates the fund-moving liquidate() function. Because AMM reserves can be shifted arbitrarily within a single transaction (classically via a flash loan, since the manipulating capital only needs to be held for the duration of one transaction), an attacker can transiently depress the reported price, call liquidate() on a solvent victim who now appears undercollateralized, and reverse the trade after collecting the victim's collateral (see the related finding on liquidate() paying out 100% of collateral with no repayment, which makes this maximally profitable). The same mechanism could instead be used to inflate price and borrow against an over-valued position. No corroborating protection (TWAP, oracle staleness window, circuit breaker) exists anywhere in the contract.
findings.recommendation: Do not price collateral from a single spot read of AMM reserves. Use a manipulation-resistant source: a multi-block time-weighted average price derived from the pair's cumulative price accumulators, a decentralized oracle feed with an on-chain staleness/deviation check, or at minimum enforce a maximum allowed single-block price deviation before accepting a new price for liquidation or borrowing decisions.

findings.description: borrow() increments borrowed[msg.sender] by any caller-supplied amount with no check against the caller's deposited collateral value and no call into isLiquidatable/any LTV cap - the debt-origination path is entirely disconnected from the collateralization ratio LIQUIDATION_THRESHOLD_BPS is meant to enforce. This is directly weaponizable, not just a theoretical gap: because Solidity 0.8's checked arithmetic reverts on overflow, a caller can call borrow() once with amount at or above type(uint256).max / 10000 (~1.157920892e73) so that debt * 10000 in isLiquidatable() always overflows and reverts. Since liquidate() calls isLiquidatable() via require, this permanently and unilaterally makes that caller's own position un-liquidatable, no matter how insolvent it becomes, because the very check meant to detect insolvency can no longer execute.
findings.recommendation: Enforce a maximum-borrow check inside borrow() itself (reject the call unless post-borrow debt keeps the account at or above the liquidation threshold, using the same valuation logic as isLiquidatable). Separately, make the isLiquidatable comparison robust against attacker-supplied magnitudes, e.g. rewrite it as debt > (collateralValue * LIQUIDATION_THRESHOLD_BPS) / 10000 so no reachable value of borrowed can force a revert and disable liquidation.

findings.description: liquidate() transfers the account's entire collateralDeposited balance to msg.sender and zeroes borrowed[account], without the caller ever repaying any portion of the outstanding debt - no asset changes hands anywhere in the contract to represent that repayment. In a conventional liquidation design, the liquidator repays some or all of the debt in the borrowed asset and receives collateral plus a bonus, with any remainder returned to the borrower. Here, the instant a position crosses the 80% threshold - even by a small margin, or as a result of the price-manipulation issue reported separately - the first caller to act receives 100% of the borrower's collateral for free and the debt is simply erased. This makes liquidation maximally punitive to borrowers and a pure, costless windfall to whoever calls it, independent of how far the position actually breached the threshold.
findings.recommendation: Require the liquidator to transfer in the debt (or the portion being liquidated) before releasing any collateral. Seize only an amount proportional to the debt repaid plus a fixed liquidation bonus (e.g. seized = debtRepaid * (1 + bonusBps/10000) / price), and return any leftover collateral to the borrower instead of paying out the full balance to the liquidator.

findings.description: The constructor stores pair into the immutable collateralPair without verifying pair != address(0). Because collateralPair can never be changed after deployment, an accidental zero-address (or otherwise invalid) argument would make every call to _currentPrice() revert (an external call to an address with no contract code reverts when Solidity tries to decode the return data), permanently disabling isLiquidatable() and liquidate() while deposit()/borrow() remain callable - i.e. collateral could be deposited and debt recorded, but the protocol could never assess or act on undercollateralized positions.
findings.recommendation: Add require(pair != address(0), "zero pair"); in the constructor, and consider verifying at deployment time that the address actually exposes a working getReserves() before accepting it.

limitations: Off-chain logic, deployment configuration and key management were not assessed.
Operational security, infrastructure and tokenomics outside the analyzed code were not assessed.
Deployed contract state and third-party systems were not assessed.

riskIndicator.explanation: This indicator reflects findings detected within the analyzed scope. It is not a measure of overall protocol security.
